etymologies.etymologyHTML: Learned borrowing from Latin radiātus, perfect passive participle of radiō (“to radiate, furnish with spokes, give out rays, radiate, shine”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from radius (“a spoke, ray”).

definitions.definition: To extend, send or spread out from a center like radii.

quote.citation: 1948 November and December, “Crewe M.P.D. to be Modernised”, in Railway Magazine, page 372:
quote.text: Crewe North Motive Power Depot is to be modernised completely. This includes the provision of a new coaling plant, ash handling plant, and two new locomotive sheds of the latest roundhouse type, each with 32 roads radiating from a 70-ft. dia. turntable.

quote.citation: 1994, Great Britain. Parliament. House of Commons, Parliamentary Debates:
quote.text: Oban is not a terminus; its routes radiate by sea, rail and road.

quote.citation: 2021 May 19, Philip Haigh, “Doncaster enhancements relying on DfT approval”, in RAIL, number 931, page 30:
quote.text: Doncaster is a rail hub in every sense. Passenger lines radiate in six directions, there are freight lines that bypass the station, extensive freight yards, a major works, and a rolling stock depot.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To come out or proceed in rays or waves.

quote.citation: 1706, John Locke, Elements of Natural Philosophy:
quote.text: Light radiates from luminous bodies directly to our eyes.

quote.citation: 1988, Douglas Adams, The Long Dark Tea-Time of the Soul, William Heinemann Ltd, page 139:
quote.text: She raised her head, and carefully opened her eyes again, staring directly into the orange glow radiating through the thick glass.

definitions.definition: To expose to ionizing radiation, such as by radiography.
(transitive) To manifest oneself in a glowing manner.

quote.citation: 1978 August 19, Harold Pickett, “New York, New York”, in Gay Community News, volume 6, number 5, page 8:
quote.text: Slim, sensual Richard Hell radiates a commanding coolness.

definitions.definition: (ecology, intransitive) To spread into new habitats, migrate.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Learned borrowing from Latin radiātus (see Etymology 1 and -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more).

definitions.definition: Radiating from a center; having rays or parts diverging from a center; radiated.
Surrounded by rays, such as the head of a saint in a religious picture; (heraldry) radiant.

quote.citation: 1915, Guy Cadogan Rothery, A. B. C. of Heraldry, page 240:
quote.text: […]  and (2) the radiate or Eastern crown, usually five rays being shown. The see of Ely bears the apocryphal coat of St. Ethelreda: gules, three open crowns or. Azure, three open crowns or, are the arms of […]

quote.citation: 2005, Rebecca R. Raines, Signal Corps, Department of the Army, page 117:
quote.text: On a wreath of the colors argent and tenné four lightning flashes barbed radiate pilewise of the first, a Roman helm or garnished gules.

definitions.definition: (botany) Having parts radiating from the center, like the petals in many flowers.
(botany) Consisting of a disc in which the florets are tubular.
(biology) Having radial symmetry, like a sea star.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From a substantivation of the above adjective through the associated taxon's name (Radiata), see -ate (noun-forming suffix).
